cells.tense: Right now the direction holds, and the hold is steady under your hand.
cells.act: let the gladness go out to the room
cells.ask: Next time something goes well, say it out loud to whoever's there while it's still warm — the small version, the good part — and watch what it does to them.
cells.core:
You can hold a chosen course out here and stay adjustable about it, which is the hard part. Something gets said that leaves you heavier, and you feel the weight, then find the one small change that puts the tune back — the timing, the amount, a different word. The course doesn't crack. It gets turned by your hands.

What this is for runs the other way too. There's gladness inside what you're carrying — a piece finished, a thing gone right between people — and it's yours to send out. Tell one person the good part, out loud, while it's still happening. What you're carrying loosens just enough for them to hold it with you, and the direction stays the one you picked.
cells.sheetLine: You hold the course and keep retuning it, which is the hard part.
cells.verb: holding the direction you chose, against what pushes back
cells.place: the place where you keep adjusting by feel — when to add, when to take away

cells.tense: In the coming stretch, the fine-tuning is already running on the next problem.
cells.act: rest in the balance you already have
cells.ask: For an hour today, stop adjusting the thing that's weighing on you. Don't solve it, don't touch it. Go do something easy instead.
cells.core:
Out here the adjusting runs past the road. There's a problem coming, and you tune for it early, then again for the one after that. You're reading resistance before it exists, working a room nobody's walked into yet, and something is getting carried around that hasn't happened.

The balance you reached is already there. Pick the thing you keep working and stay off it for one hour: not solved, not abandoned, just untouched. Go do something easy, no purpose in it. What's already set doesn't need you leaning on it, and the hour you spend away will tell you what actually wants your hands.
cells.sheetLine: You're tuning for the next room before you've walked in.
cells.verb: holding the direction you chose, against what pushes back

cells.tense: The hold has been put down, and the feet are still at the old step.
cells.ask: Name the shape that formed after the last ending — the one already setting in — and give it one plain thing that keeps it going this week.
cells.core:
Out here the strength to hold a direction is intact; what's missing is a thing to hold. The old stance is still being stood in, the stance you had before the ground changed. You go back to it out of habit, and the habit takes the spot something current could stand in.

What your strength is good for is what a change left behind. Something shifted, put plainly, and it left a form: the better hour, the full night's sleep, the two of you talking straight. Name it, then give it one plain thing this week that keeps it going. Holding a form is what your hands already know how to do.
cells.sheetLine: The strength is here, the thing to hold has gone quiet.

cells.tense: The adjusting is running, steady through the day's beat, and you'd say it's just how things are.
cells.act: build the first new thing from what the clearing showed
cells.ask: Make one small new thing on ground that's already clear — the first piece of the version you'd actually pick — and keep it to yourself until it stands.
cells.core:
Somewhere out here you've been keeping a course that matters to you, one adjustment at a time, through days that don't announce it. Asked, you'd say you were managing, getting through the week. In fact you've been keeping the direction and retuning it all the while, and none of it shows from outside as yours.

That's not a lack. Adjusting is older than the start of anything — you were doing it before you could have named a reason. Stand on the cleared ground and make the first new piece with your hands: the honest version of the thing, small, nobody needing to see it yet. When it stands, noticing does the rest.
cells.sheetLine: You keep a course one small turn at a time, and call it getting by.

A reader could object that the Too Little version locates a whole stuck life rather than one capacity in one part of it; I've kept it to where the strength stands, not why, and left out any account of what happened. The asks survive a wrong read: each comes from the medicine's own listed acts and is small enough to be useful whether or not my picture fits. The line that serves me more than them is the Too Much scaffold image — I've cut the metaphor down to walking and held it to one carried thing so it stays their life, not my figure.
